remedial-massage: Remedial massage is the massage your health fund still recognises — which is the practical difference between it and a relaxation massage booked under the same roof. The therapist holds a diploma rather than a certificate, works to what you asked for at the start rather than to a set routine, and the session tends to be firmer and more local than a flowing full-body treatment. The two can happen on the same table in the same hour; the name tells you about the training behind the hands and whether a receipt is worth keeping.

Sessions run thirty, sixty or ninety minutes in a private room. You will be asked what you want before anyone touches you — answer properly, because that conversation decides how the rest of the hour goes — and you stay covered by a towel, undressed only as far as you are comfortable. Asking for less pressure is normal and nobody minds. In Perth the same clinics commonly add dry needling, cupping or a sports massage to the menu, and a good share of them also book pregnancy massage, which needs its own table setup and is worth saying when you ring, not when you arrive.

Two things to check before you book rather than after: whether the therapist holds a provider number your fund recognises, and — in a clinic with several rooms — whether the therapist you booked is the therapist you will actually get. Extras are priced separately almost everywhere, so a session that starts as massage and ends with needles costs more than the number on the website.
pilates: The first thing to sort out is reformer or mat, because they are priced, booked and taught differently. Reformer classes use the spring-loaded machine, run in small groups because there are only so many beds in the room, and almost every studio will put you through a foundation class or two before letting you into the general timetable — not an upsell, just how the machine is taught. Mat classes need none of that, take more people, and cost noticeably less.

Around those two sit the variations you will see on Perth timetables: barre borrowing from ballet, floor-based strength classes, mums-and-bubs terms, and clinical Pilates run by physiotherapists one-to-one or in twos and threes. The clinical kind matters for one dull reason — since 2019 private health funds no longer rebate Pilates as a natural therapy, and the exception is when a physiotherapist delivers it as physiotherapy. Ask which you are booking if the rebate matters to you.

Reformer studios generally ask for grip socks, and sell them at the desk if you arrive without. Class sizes are small enough that popular times book out days ahead. Almost every studio runs an introductory offer for new students, which is the cheapest way to try two or three rooms before you commit to a membership you then have to use.
infrared-sauna: An infrared sauna is a cabin heated by panels rather than a stove, which makes it noticeably cooler and drier than a traditional Finnish room — warm enough to sweat in, cool enough to read in. You sit for somewhere between twenty and forty-five minutes and that is the whole activity. Most Perth studios book the cabin privately rather than as a shared bench, so what you wear is your own business and a phone or a book is fine.

It is rarely sold on its own. In Perth it sits on the menu of recovery studios beside ice baths, contrast sessions that move you between hot and cold on a timer, red light panels and compression boots, and the pricing reflects that — a single session, a pack of ten, or a monthly pass that only makes sense if you turn up every week. A handful of float centres and day spas run one as an add-on to something else.

Bring thongs, a towel and water rather than assuming the studio supplies them. A first visit runs longer than the booked slot because someone has to show you the room. Studios that take walk-ins are the exception, and the evening and weekend slots are the ones that fill.
naturopathy: A first naturopathy consultation is long — an hour to ninety minutes is normal — and it is mostly questions: history, diet, sleep, what you have already tried. Follow-ups are shorter. Some practitioners work from a clinic room, some from a room at home, and a fair share of those listed here consult by video, which matters if the person you want is on the other side of the river.

Naturopaths are not registered with AHPRA, the national scheme that covers doctors, physiotherapists and Chinese medicine practitioners. The field regulates itself through professional associations such as ANTA and the NHAA, so the practitioner's association membership and their actual qualifications are the things there are to check, and both are reasonable to ask about before you book. Since 2019 private health funds have not paid rebates on naturopathy, so assume you are paying in full.

Practitioners who dispense herbs or supplements almost always charge for them separately from the consultation, and that is where the cost of a course sits. It is fair to ask what a month would come to before you agree to anything. Functional testing, where offered, is priced on top again.
Oria Haven is a directory, not a health service. If you have a health concern, speak with your GP or a registered practitioner.
acupuncture: Acupuncturists in Australia are registered with AHPRA through the Chinese Medicine Board, the same national register that covers doctors and physiotherapists, and any practitioner listed here can be looked up by name. That registration is the useful fact about the whole category: it is what separates acupuncture from most of the other things in this directory, and it is why many health-fund extras policies still cover it.

A session runs forty-five minutes to an hour, the first one longer because it starts with questions. You lie on a treatment table, the needles are fine, single-use and sterile, and the part people do not expect is that most of the session is spent lying still with them in — twenty minutes or so, in a quiet room, often with the lights down. Perth clinics commonly offer cupping and Chinese herbal medicine under the same roof, and some pair acupuncture with remedial massage.

Wear something loose enough to roll above the knee and the elbow, eat something beforehand, and allow a little more time than the booking says. If your fund matters to you, ask the clinic for its provider number when you book rather than at the counter.
Oria Haven is a directory, not a health service. If you have a health concern, speak with your GP or a registered practitioner.
sound-healing: A sound bath is a room of mats, blankets and instruments — gongs, crystal or Tibetan bowls, sometimes chimes — played around and over you while you lie still. There is no water involved at any point, which nobody says and everybody quietly wonders about. You keep your clothes on, nothing is required of you, and you can leave whenever you like.

In Perth it mostly lives inside yoga studios and wellness spaces rather than in rooms of its own: an evening session after the last class, a Sunday morning, a full-moon or end-of-month event. Some pair the sound with yin yoga, yoga nidra or a breathwork session in the same sitting. Because so much of it runs as one-off events rather than a weekly timetable, the what's-on pages are often the better place to look than a studio's regular schedule.

Bring a blanket and an eye pillow if you run cold or like the dark, arrive ten minutes early because the door tends to close when the instruments start, and expect somewhere between forty-five and seventy-five minutes on the floor. Mats are usually supplied.
wellness-retreats: Retreats near Perth divide by how long you stay and how much of the day somebody else decides. Day retreats run a single day — usually a Saturday — and combine a couple of sessions with a meal, which makes them the low-commitment end and the place to start. Residential retreats run a weekend or longer at properties in the Perth Hills, out past Serpentine, up the Swan Valley and down the coast, with meals and a set timetable included.

Silent retreats are their own proposition: several days without conversation, phones handed in or left off, long stretches of sitting, and an end-of-retreat evening where everyone talks at once. Some meditation centres also run free introductory days and talks, which are the cheapest way to find out whether the longer kind is for you before you book a week of it.

Popular weekends book months ahead, so a same-day booking is optimistic. Almost everything here is a driving trip, and the properties are rarely walkable to anything else. Check what is included before comparing prices — accommodation, meals and sessions are bundled differently by nearly every venue, and a single-room supplement is common.
